title: The Occupancy Illusion: Why a Fully Booked December Doesn't Guarantee a Profitable One for Accommodation Operators
excerpt: Accommodation operators watch occupancy climb every December and assume profit follows. The margin story behind a fully booked Christmas and New Year peak usually tells a different one.
content:
Every accommodation operator along the Queensland, New South Wales and Victorian coastline is watching the same number climb through November. By the second week of December, most beachside motels, holiday parks and boutique stays are booked solid through to late January. In revenue terms, it is usually the best six weeks of the trading year.

The profit story rarely matches the occupancy story. A property running at ninety per cent occupancy over the Christmas and New Year peak can post a thinner margin than a quiet shoulder season month, because the cost of filling the last rooms at peak is higher than the cost of filling the rooms that were always easy to sell. Occupancy tells an owner how full the property is. It does not tell them what any of those nights actually kept.

The gap usually sits in three places most accommodation operators never model before the season starts: what each booking nets once the channel that brought it takes its cut, what it costs in wages and consumables to service a fully occupied property across a run of public holidays, and what gets quietly deferred into the new year because there was no capacity to deal with it during the rush.

The rate the booking platform doesn't show you

Occupancy is the number most owners watch first. Average daily rate net of commission is the number that actually determines profit, and it is rarely the same figure. A booking through a major online travel agency can carry a commission in the order of fifteen to twenty per cent before the room has even been cleaned. Add in the last minute discount used to fill the final few rooms in a property that was already close to full, and the real average daily rate for the peak period often sits well below the rack rate printed on the listing. An occupancy report that doesn't separate direct bookings from third party channel bookings, and doesn't net out commission before counting revenue, is measuring how busy the property looks rather than what it actually earned.

Peak season staffing costs more per room than shoulder season staffing does

A fully booked property over Christmas and New Year needs more housekeeping turns, more laundry cycles and faster maintenance response than the same property running at sixty per cent occupancy in April. It also needs that labour on exactly the days penalty rates are highest. The marginal cost of servicing the last ten per cent of occupancy, the handful of rooms that push a property from comfortably full to completely full, is frequently higher than the revenue those rooms bring in once wages, laundry and consumables are counted against them properly. Most operators still price every room at the same rate regardless of which week it falls in, which means the rooms sold into the most expensive labour week are often the least profitable ones in the calendar.

What the rush quietly defers

The weeks either side of Christmas rarely leave room for anything beyond running the property. Maintenance that should happen between guests gets pushed to January. Reconciling what each channel actually paid gets pushed to February. Repricing for the next peak gets pushed to whenever someone finds the time, which in practice means it happens too late to change anything. By the time the next BAS is due, the business is reconciling a season nobody actually reviewed while it was happening, and the leave accrued by casual and seasonal staff over the rush is sitting on the balance sheet as a surprise rather than a plan.

None of this means a strong peak season is a bad one. It usually isn't. It means the number worth tracking through November and December is not how full the calendar looks, but what each booking nets once the channel fee, the labour cost and the deferred work are counted against it. That is a line by line review of channel and room type margin, which is exactly the shape of work a Cost & Margin Deep Dive is built to do, and it matters more for accommodation operators across the Sunshine Coast and the wider Queensland coast in the six weeks before Christmas than at almost any other point in the year. The operators who come out of January with a clear year ahead are usually the ones who built real cash flow discipline into the season before it started, not the ones who waited to see how the numbers landed.

faqs.q: Why doesn't high occupancy always mean high profit for accommodation businesses?
faqs.a: Occupancy measures how full a property is, not what each booking actually nets. Once commissions, peak season wages and consumables are counted against a room, a fully booked week over Christmas can return a thinner margin than a quieter month. The pattern is common across accommodation operators, which is why a Cost & Margin Deep Dive looks at channel and room type profitability separately from occupancy.

faqs.q: How much commission do booking platforms typically take from accommodation operators?
faqs.a: Commission rates vary by platform and the agreement in place, but a meaningful share of each booking, often in the order of fifteen to twenty per cent, is common for major online travel agencies. That fee comes out before the property sees a cent, which is why the rate printed on a listing is rarely the rate that actually lands in the bank account.

faqs.q: Why do peak season staffing costs eat into accommodation profit margins?
faqs.a: A fully occupied property over Christmas and New Year needs more housekeeping, laundry and maintenance response on exactly the days penalty rates are highest. The last rooms sold into a near full calendar are often the most expensive to service, which means the final stretch of occupancy can add less to profit than the headline revenue suggests.

faqs.q: Should accommodation operators forecast cash flow through the Christmas and New Year peak?
faqs.a: Yes. Peak season brings its own cash timing, with wages, commissions and supplier costs often moving faster than the cash actually clears from bookings taken months earlier. Building cash flow discipline before the season starts gives an owner a clearer picture of what the peak will actually leave behind once it is over.

faqs.q: What is RevPAR and why does it matter more than occupancy alone?
faqs.a: RevPAR, or revenue per available room, combines occupancy and average daily rate into a single figure, which makes it a better measure of performance than occupancy on its own. A property can lift occupancy by discounting rooms and still see RevPAR fall, because the extra bookings are being sold at a lower net rate than the rooms that were already filling.

faqs.q: How can an accommodation business improve its margin without cutting its rates?
faqs.a: The most reliable lever is usually channel mix rather than price. Shifting bookings toward direct channels reduces commission leakage without touching the rate a guest actually pays, and reviewing which room types and booking windows carry the lowest net margin often reveals where discounting has become automatic rather than deliberate.

faqs.q: Does a strong peak season actually improve what an accommodation business is worth?
faqs.a: Only if the margin behind the occupancy is real and can be shown consistently across seasons. Buyers and valuers look at normalised earnings rather than booking calendars, so a property that can demonstrate disciplined channel and cost management through its peak is in a stronger position than one relying on a busy look alone.
